event.title: Root cause: no consolidated version
event.description: The corpus only holds the original version: amendments are published as separate laws and no consolidated, machine-readable version is available.

responses.message:
The Constitution of the Republic of Cameroon is published in its original text of 1996. The amendments adopted by the law n° 2008/001 (and later by law n° 2026/002) are issued as separate legislative acts, but no official consolidated version that integrates those amendments into a single, updated text is provided by the State.  

**What this means for you**

1. **Consult the original Constitution** – the text you find in the official gazette of 1996 (e.g., the excerpts you have in [1] and [3]).  
2. **Consult the amendment laws** – read law n° 2008/001 (Article premier) and law n° 2026/002 for the modifications to the articles mentioned in the note of version. These laws are published separately in the Journal Officiel.  
3. **Cross‑check the two sources** – when you need the current wording of a specific article, compare the original article with the changes introduced by the amendment laws.  

**Where to verify**

- The **Journal Officiel du Cameroun** (official gazette) – contains the full text of law n° 2008/001 and law n° 2026/002.  
- The **website of the Ministry of Justice** or the **National Assembly** – often provides PDFs of the original Constitution and of each amendment law.  

**Legal gap**

The legal framework does not provide a single, officially consolidated Constitution that incorporates the 2008 (and later 2026) revisions. Users must piece together the current law from the original Constitution and the separate amendment texts. This lack of consolidation can create practical difficulties in identifying the exact current wording of constitutional provisions.

gaps.title: No consolidated, machine-readable legal texts
gaps.description: Amendments are published as separate acts; there is no official consolidated version of each article with its validity dates, in an open format. Neither a citizen nor an AI assistant can reliably tell which version is in force.
gaps.globalExample: France: Légifrance publishes consolidated versions of codes and laws with their validity dates, also as open data (DILA). European Union: EUR-Lex publishes consolidated versions of legal acts.
